Complex Rate Structures

Demand Charges

Hidden Fees & Riders

REFERENCE DOCUMENTATION

Bill Component Library

Comprehensive explanations of commercial utility billing components, rate structures, and optimization strategies.

Bill Line Items

  • Kilowatt-hour (kWh)

    A kilowatt-hour is 1000 watts drawn for one hour; it measures energy used, not the rate of use.

  • Therm

    A therm is 100,000 BTU of heat energy and appears on gas bills; electric bills use kWh instead.

  • Billing demand (kW)

    Billing demand is the highest average power draw over a short interval in the period, billed separately from energy.

  • Load factor

    Load factor is average demand divided by peak demand for the period; a low ratio means short spikes drive the bill.

  • Demand ratchet clause

    A ratchet clause sets billed demand to a floor based on an earlier peak, so a quiet month can still carry a summer charge.

  • Power factor penalty

    Some commercial tariffs adjust billing when power factor falls below a stated threshold, because reactive current loads the network.

Rate Structures

  • Flat small-commercial plan, no demand charge

    The simplest commercial design prices every kWh the same and adds a fixed monthly charge, with no separate peak penalty.

  • Small-commercial time-of-use, no demand charge

    Energy price varies by hour while demand is not billed separately, so scheduling matters and short spikes do not.

  • Small-commercial time-of-use with demand charge

    Both the hour of use and the highest short-interval draw are priced, so two separate levers appear on one bill.

  • Medium-commercial TOU with demand ratchet

    Billed demand carries a floor tied to an earlier peak, which decouples winter charges from winter behaviour.

TECHNICAL QUESTIONS

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did my bill increase despite lower consumption?

Demand charges are calculated based on your highest 15-minute interval demand, not total monthly consumption. A single peak event can disproportionately impact your bill.

What distinguishes supply from delivery charges?

Supply represents the commodity cost of electricity generation. Delivery covers transmission and distribution infrastructure. In deregulated markets, supply may be shoppable.

Can I change my rate schedule?

Most commercial customers qualify for multiple rate schedules. Optimal selection depends on load factor, peak demand timing, and seasonal usage patterns.
